entry.title: Blade Blitz @ Hella Studios
entry.content:
Blade Blitz is a competitive local-multiplayer sword fighting game inspired by Nidhogg, reimagined as a fast-paced 3v3 spectator sport. I designed and developed it from the ground up—visual identity, UI/UX, characters, and full Unity implementation—over two years of public iteration.

Timeline
Q1 2024 - March 2026

Outcome

Blade Blitz launched on Steam on March 11, 2026. Two years of public development, event showcases, and direct player feedback shaped what shipped.

1,000+
Wishlists at Launch
Blade Blitz launched on Steam on March 11, 2026, surpassing 1,000 wishlists at release—meaningful for a solo title without a publisher.
350+
Demo Players
The standalone Steam demo reached over 350 players ahead of the full release.
Shipped solo
Every system—design, code, art, and marketing—was owned and shipped by one person.

Visual System

The visual system is built across three layers: the overall aesthetic, character readability, and a scalable UI component library, each designed to support clarity in fast-paced, competitive gameplay.

Sports-inspired aesthetic
BBold typography, high-contrast team colors (red vs. blue), and clear iconography create immediate readability, allowing players and spectators to quickly understand the state of play at a glance.
Character design
3D characters modeled in Blender for legibility from a top-down perspective, with per-team color assignment built into the outline shader.
Component system
A consistent UI library covering buttons, panels, HUD elements, and feedback states, designed in Figma and implemented directly in Unity.

Interface Design

The interface applies the component system across all screens, ensuring consistency, clarity, and scalability throughout the experience.

Menu
Menu screens use a consistent layout structure built from reusable panels and button components.
Character select
Character select extends the same component system into a more dynamic, multiplayer context.
In-match UI
The in-match HUD adapts the system for moment-to-moment gameplay.
Feedback & States
Interactive and game-driven feedback—hover states, selections, alerts, and transitions—are all derived from the same component rules.

Playtesting & Showcase

Public events were the primary testing environment. Hours of unmoderated player sessions at ECCC and the Seattle Indie Expo 2025 exposed friction that internal playtesting never surfaces—watching someone play for the first time, with no context or instruction, was consistently the most useful design signal available.

Reflection

This project surfaced a few hard lessons around product direction and scope.

Platform fit matters more than technical possibility
I built the game around local multiplayer, assuming Steam Remote Play would fill the gap. In practice, it didn't. Players still prefer native online experiences. If I were to do it again, I would design for online play from the start rather than relying on a workaround.
Novelty is expensive, especially twice
The game introduced both unfamiliar controls and unfamiliar rules. That combination made onboarding difficult and made it harder to communicate the concept quickly. I'd approach this differently by grounding one layer (controls or rules) in something familiar, so players have an anchor.
Perfection can become a trap
As development progressed, the bar kept rising. Instead of converging, the scope expanded toward perfect, which slowed decision making and shipping. In hindsight, I would define clearer constraints earlier and commit to them.
entry.summary: Blade Blitz is a competitive local-multiplayer sword fighting game inspired by Nidhogg, reimagined as a fast-paced 3v3 spectator sport. I designed and developed it from the ground up—visual identity, UI/UX, characters, and full Unity implementation—over two years of public iteration.

entry.title: BitCraft Online @ Clockwork Labs
entry.content:
BitCraft Online posed a clear design challenge. Build a comprehensive UI system for a massively multiplayer game with deep simulation systems and a persistent open world. I defined the visual identity from the ground up, an art deco-inspired design language spanning type, color, spacing, and a full component library. Beyond the design itself, I built the handoff process between design and engineering, and extended the work into marketing and brand assets for TwitchCon and Steam.

Morgan Nyblom (Art Director)
Lisandro Crespo (UI Engineer)

Context

BitCraft Online is a sandbox MMO built around player-driven worldbuilding: exploration, survival, crafting, and a persistent open world shaped by its community. Designing UI for a game at this scale means solving for information density first. Players are managing inventory, tracking progression, coordinating with others, and interacting with simulation systems simultaneously. The interface cannot afford to be slow, cluttered, or inconsistent. The starting point was establishing a visual identity strong enough to unify every surface, then building the component system to deliver it across the full game.

Outcome

BitCraft Online launched into early access and found an audience. The numbers reflect both the strength of the product and the sustained community work that preceded launch.

250,000+
Wishlists
BitCraft Online accumulated over 250,000 wishlists ahead of launch, a strong signal of community interest built through consistent public presence and marketing.
4,500+
Daily CCU at Launch
BitCraft Online launched with over 4,500 concurrent players daily, a strong retention signal for an independent early access MMO.
127,000+
Copies Sold
As of March 2026, BitCraft Online has sold an estimated 127,000+ copies on Steam, a meaningful result for an independent studio's early access title.

Visual Identity

The foundation of BitCraft's visual language is an art deco-inspired design system built for density and clarity:

Color Palette
The palette uses a split complementary system, two colors flanking the complementary of the primary, creating visual harmony without monotony. Each primary has tonal variants for layering, segmentation, and subtle UI patterning. A light and dark mode support both casual and low-light play sessions.
Typography & Spacing
The type ramp is built on a 14px base with an augmented fourth scale (1.414), calibrated for information-dense interfaces where hierarchy needs to be legible without oversized headers competing with game data. An 8pt spacing grid brings rhythm to component layout and padding throughout.
Shape Language
The visual language draws from art deco geometry: precise angles, intersecting lines at 45 and 30 degrees, and a strict use of 4px and 8px stroke weights for dividers and framing elements. This gives the interface a structural consistency that reads as crafted rather than generic.

Interface Design

With the visual system defined, every UI surface needed to be built from it. The goal was a component library comprehensive enough to handle the full range of MMO interactions without requiring one-off solutions:

Component Library
Built to cover the full range of MMO interaction contexts, from inventory and crafting to dialogue and progression. Every component draws from the same visual system to keep the interface coherent regardless of context.
Windows & Panels
Modular window and panel system designed to handle dense information loads without visual noise. Built to accommodate the game's layered simulation systems.
HUD
The in-game heads-up display keeps critical information accessible during active play without occluding the game world. Designed to scale with gameplay complexity as players progress.
Notifications & Feedback
A notification system covering both inline and side-panel variants, providing contextual feedback for a world where dozens of concurrent systems are always running.
Cursors & Entities
Contextual cursor states and entity display patterns that communicate interactable objects, NPCs, and player characters at a glance in a populated open world.

Marketing & Brand

The visual identity extended beyond the game itself. BitCraft's presence at TwitchCon 2025 and on Steam required assets that carried the same design language into physical and marketing contexts:

TwitchCon 2025 Booth
Designed and modeled a 3D preview of the TwitchCon 2025 booth, giving the team a concrete visual to plan the physical presence around.
TwitchCon Merchandise
Designed and mocked the TwitchCon 2025 hoodie, creating a wearable that carries the BitCraft visual identity beyond the screen.
Steam & Social Assets
Created wishlist campaign assets and templates for the marketing team, enabling consistent, high-quality output across YouTube, Steam, and social channels.
entry.summary: BitCraft Online posed a clear design challenge. Build a comprehensive UI system for a massively multiplayer game with deep simulation systems and a persistent open world. I defined the visual identity from the ground up, an art deco-inspired design language spanning type, color, spacing, and a full component library. Beyond the design itself, I built the handoff process between design and engineering, and extended the work into marketing and brand assets for TwitchCon and Steam.

entry.title: SpacetimeDB @ Clockwork Labs
entry.content:
SpacetimeDB had a visual identity when I joined Clockwork Labs. It was a dark, space-inspired aesthetic with a green accent and strong marketing presence. My role was to take that foundation and build a full developer portal. After shipping that, feedback from investors and users gave me the opening to go back and formalize the visual system, introducing a proper type ramp, extending the radial language, tightening spacing, and recalibrating the color palette.
SpacetimeDB Websitearrow_outward
Client
Clockwork Labs
Skills
UI/UX Design
Branding
Motion Design
3D
Tools
Figma
Blender
After Effects
My Role
Product Designer
Timeline
Q3 2024 – Present
Team
Tyler Cloutier (Co-Founder & CEO)
Alessandro Asoni (Co-Founder & CTO)

Context

SpacetimeDB is a distributed database built for real-time multiplayer games. It handles server-side logic natively, removing the need for a separate game server. The brand was already established when I came on: a dark aesthetic, a distinctive green accent, and a marketing site. What was missing was the product itself. There was the skeleton of a developer portal, no formalized design system, and no type or spacing standards. My starting point was to build the portal from that foundation, then work backward to formalize the system that should have existed underneath it.

Outcome

The portal gave SpacetimeDB a complete developer product experience for the first time. The system work that followed gave it a foundation solid enough to build from.

75,000+
Registered Users
As of March 2026, SpacetimeDB has surpassed 75,000 registered users, a strong signal of developer adoption for an early-stage infrastructure product.
A Portal Built for Developers
The developer portal shipped as a complete, designed product experience, from first login through day-to-day database management.
A Formalized Visual System
What was previously an intuitive brand became a documented system: defined type scales, spacing rules, color roles, and component patterns that any future designer or engineer can work from.
Ongoing Ownership
As the sole designer, I continue to drive the design direction across both product and brand as SpacetimeDB grows.

Typography & Spacing

The absence of a type ramp was the most felt gap in the portal. I introduced a formal scale:

14px Base, 1.200 Scale
Portal screens are content-dense (tables, metrics, code), so the type ramp needed more steps at smaller sizes. A minor third scale (1.200) from a 14px base created the visual hierarchy without forcing oversized headers that compete with data.
Consistent Type Styles
Defined a set of named styles (headings, labels, body, caption, code) so every surface in the portal draws from the same system rather than ad-hoc sizing decisions.
Spacing via 8pt Grid
Applied an 8pt grid throughout to bring rhythm to component spacing, padding, and layout gaps. This was especially impactful in the tables and metrics views where density makes inconsistency obvious.

Visual Language & Color

Beyond type, the visual refinement touched three areas that were affecting cohesion and usability:

Radial Patterns
The brand already had a radial motif in the hero, but it hadn't been extended further. I developed a broader library of radial elements to bring that language into the portal and supporting surfaces, making it feel like a system rather than a one-off detail.
Color Recalibration
The original dark background used near-black against near-white text, which was too high contrast for extended reading in a developer tool. I shifted the neutrals lighter with a cool tone, reducing harshness while keeping the dark aesthetic and letting the green accent read more naturally against it.
Component Sizing
Buttons and interactive elements were sized for information-dense screens, smaller than typical to keep them proportional to the data they sit alongside without sacrificing touch targets or legibility.
entry.summary: SpacetimeDB had a visual identity when I joined Clockwork Labs. It was a dark, space-inspired aesthetic with a green accent and strong marketing presence. My role was to take that foundation and build a full developer portal. After shipping that, feedback from investors and users gave me the opening to go back and formalize the visual system, introducing a proper type ramp, extending the radial language, tightening spacing, and recalibrating the color palette.

entry.title: Boss Fight
entry.content:
I created an entry for the Boss Fight 3D challenge, where artists were given a starter template and tasked with animating a scene featuring a hero facing a towering villain. Similar to the Endless Engines challenge, this project pushed me to practice modeling, texturing, rigging, and animation within a focused brief, while experimenting with scale, character dynamics, and storytelling through motion.

  • Built and maintained the shared Figma design library, enabling the team to scale efficiently, iterate faster, and maintain visual cohesion across a large, multi-studio production.

entry.summary: I was a UI/UX Designer on Silent Hill Ascension, a new form of interactive entertainment developed by Genvid that blended television with gaming. The experience allowed viewers to participate in live storylines by playing minigames to earn points, which were then used to vote on key narrative decisions. Votes were tallied weekly, with the story progressing based on community input. My role was to design the user experience and interface systems that supported this hybrid format, ensuring gameplay, voting, and storytelling were intuitive and engaging for a global audience.

entry.content:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, I challenged myself to learn Blender by modeling and rendering different sections of my apartment. Working in an orthographic perspective, I treated each room as both a design study and a storytelling canvas.

Context

During the COVID-19 lockdown, I used the time to learn Blender from scratch. Rather than following tutorials, I set myself a concrete project: model and render the spaces I was living in. entry.title: Stream Pirates @ Captain.tv
entry.content:
Stream Pirates was a Twitch-integrated idle strategy game where a streamer's live audience became their army—raiding islands, collecting loot, and driving gameplay in real time through chat commands. A streamer would run the game as a persistent side layer during their broadcast—viewers joined via chat commands, formed crews, and raided islands together. The game needed to work visually on stream, in a browser, and feel native to the pirate theme without being generic.

Outcome

The visual system shipped with the game and held up through an active closed beta.

1,000+
Peak Concurrent Viewers
Reached over 1,000 concurrent viewers on Twitch during peak gameplay sessions.
30+
Streamers in Closed Beta
Played by 30+ streamers simultaneously during the closed beta, stress-testing the live gameplay systems.
Cohesive UI/UX direction
Unified pixel gameplay with character-driven key art, implemented directly in Unity to accelerate development.
Built for live audiences
Designed for Twitch partners and affiliates, enabling real-time audience participation through chat-driven gameplay.

Visual Direction

I ran a broad exploration across color palettes, typography, component shapes, and HUD paradigms before settling on a hybrid direction. Pixel textures grounded the UI in the gameplay world. Painted, slightly worn surfaces—parchment, wood grain, aged metal—bridged toward the illustrated key art. The result felt like a single world, not a collision of two production pipelines.

UI System

Once the direction was locked, I built out the full component library: buttons, containers, parchment panels, tooltips, icons, inputs, and the battle pass. Each component was designed to work at stream resolution—readable when compressed and overlaid on gameplay, not just in Figma at full scale.

Twitch Interaction

The in-game screens were the surface players actually saw during a stream. They needed to carry the brand while keeping gameplay readable in the background. I designed each screen to minimize screen real estate and keep the viewer's attention on the action—not the UI chrome.
